title: Constant acceleration (SUVAT)
examples: What is the difference between constant and non-constant acceleration?
How do I use the SUVAT equations when the object is thrown upwards?
Can I use these equations if the starting velocity is not given?

explain.say: Today we look at constant acceleration using SUVAT equations. These equations help us find motion details. We use them when acceleration is steady throughout the journey.

draw.text: SUVAT: v, u, a, t, s

explain.say: The first step is choosing the right equation. You must know what values you have and what you need to find. Remember the variables stand for final velocity, initial velocity, acceleration, time, and displacement.
Next we look at vertical motion under gravity. Gravity causes a constant downward acceleration. On Earth, this acceleration is about nine point eight meters per second squared.
When an object moves vertically upwards, its final velocity at its highest point is zero. This is a key point for solving these problems. We can use this fact to find the time taken.

items: Use this fact to find time

faq.q: What is the value for the acceleration due to gravity?
faq.a: The standard value for acceleration due to gravity is nine point eight meters per second squared. Remember that this value is always directed downwards.
asks: What is the acceleration from gravity?

faq.q: When do I use the SUVAT equations?
faq.a: You use them only when the acceleration is constant throughout the motion. If the acceleration changes, these equations will not work correctly.

faq.q: How do I handle the direction of motion?
faq.a: It is best practice to set up a coordinate system. If up is positive, then acceleration due to gravity must be negative. This keeps your calculations consistent.
asks: Should I use positive or negative for g?
How do I account for direction?

faq.q: What does 'u' stand for in these equations?
faq.a: The letter u always stands for the initial velocity. This is the velocity the object has at the very beginning of the time interval you are studying.

faq.q: If I find the time to reach maximum height, what is the final velocity?
faq.a: At the very peak of its flight, the object momentarily stops before falling back down. Therefore, its final velocity at that exact point is zero.
asks: What is the speed at the top?
Does the velocity equal zero at the peak?

facts: SUVAT equations apply only when acceleration is constant.
Acceleration due to gravity, g, is approximately nine point eight meters per second squared.
When an object reaches its maximum height, its instantaneous vertical velocity is zero.
If up is positive, the acceleration due to gravity (g) must be treated as negative.

quiz.say: A ball is thrown upwards with an initial velocity of twenty meters per second. What is its velocity at the peak?

options.show: nine point eight meters per second squared
options.say: nine point eight meters per second squared

quiz.why: At the maximum height, the object momentarily stops moving before falling, so its final velocity is zero.

wrong.0: The negative sign suggests it is moving downwards, but at the peak, it is momentarily stationary.
wrong.1: This is the acceleration due to gravity, not the velocity.
wrong.3: This is the initial velocity, not the velocity at the peak.

quiz.say: A stone is dropped from a building. If we take downwards as positive, what is the acceleration?

options.show: -nine point eight meters per second squared
options.say: -nine point eight meters per second squared

options.show: nine point eight divided by two
options.say: nine point eight divided by two

options.show: nine point eight meters per second squared
options.say: nine point eight meters per second squared

quiz.why: Since we defined downwards as positive, the acceleration due to gravity takes the positive value of nine point eight.

wrong.0: The stone is accelerating due to gravity, so the acceleration is not zero.
wrong.1: This would be correct if we defined upwards as positive, but we defined downwards as positive.
wrong.2: There is no reason to divide the acceleration by two in this scenario.

quiz.say: A rocket is launched upwards. If it reaches a height of fifty meters in four seconds, what was its average acceleration?

options.show: eight point two meters per second squared
options.say: eight point two meters per second squared

quiz.why: We use the equation s = ut + one half at squared. Plugging in the values gives us the required acceleration.

wrong.0: This incorrectly assumes the initial velocity was zero and the final velocity was twenty.
wrong.1: This incorrectly adds the initial velocity to the acceleration.
wrong.3: This calculates average velocity, not the constant acceleration.
